Of this share, a significant portion lies in the central core of Tehran, including Districts 6, 7, 11, and 12, where people currently make these short trips by motorcycle or taxi, though they could potentially be made by shared bicycles. Moreover, under current conditions, the central area of Tehran sees a significant volume of motorcycles moving around for daily trips, and as a result of this heavy traffic, we are witnessing chaos, reduced safety, collisions with pedestrians, disruption of safe movement, and so on.Given that Tehran's public transportation system does not operate in an integrated manner and the first and last kilometers of trips often require citizens to cover considerable distances to reach public transit stations, establishing a shared bicycle system in the central core of cities can alleviate part of this problem and facilitate getting to public transportation or from public transportation to one's final destination.Given the country's current circumstances and the two recent wars that have made the issue of fuel imbalance more serious, as well as the importance of infrastructure and the likelihood that infrastructure may become unavailable, and on the other hand, the issue of passive defense, which has not received sufficient attention in the transportation sector, the importance of establishing a shared bicycle system in Tehran becomes far greater. This is because the shared bicycle system, with no dependence on fuel, at low cost, and with far less dependence on transportation infrastructure, can make short trips possible under critical conditions and also enable trips to shelters (in critical conditions).📰 This note, titled "Shared bikes still at a crossroads: good or bad," has been published in the Shargh newspaper:https://www.sharghdaily.com/fa/tiny/news-1130470

entry.title: [darvishnameh] 🔶 Mohammad Darvish: Desalinating Oman Sea water is choosing between bad and…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @darvishnameh

🔶 Mohammad Darvish: Desalinating Oman Sea water is choosing between bad and worse

The government of Masoud Pezeshkian inaugurated the first phase of the project to transfer water from the Oman Sea to the Central Plateau on the 15th of Azar — a plan that Isfahan's industries see as a lifesaver, but some experts warn about its environmental consequences, its energy intensity, and the threat it poses to the Makran coast.

In this context, Mohammad Darvish, an environmental activist, stressed in an interview with Deutsche Welle Persian that "implementing the desalination project for the Oman Sea and transferring water to Isfahan could have far fewer adverse environmental and security consequences than implementing projects to transfer water from the headwaters of the Karun and Dez to Isfahan."

He added: "Unfortunately, the insistence on carrying out projects such as Cheshmeh Langan and Khodangestan and drying up two headwaters of the Dez River, pursuing destructive projects such as the Mandegan Dam and diverting the Marbor River from the headwaters of the Karun, the Khersan 3 Dam and the Beheshtabad project, the plan to transfer water from the Zayandeh Rud to Yazd, and drawing water from the Zayandeh Rud to develop certain orchards have dealt the biggest blow to the resilience of the Dez, Karun, and Zayandeh Rud watersheds and have fueled widespread discontent in the region."

Darvish concludes that "desalinating sea water itself has worrisome environmental consequences, but when choosing between bad and worse, it is preferable."

At the same time, this environmental activist warns that "this water should not be spent on further industrial development and implementing more projects in Isfahan," and adds: "Additional pressure on the provinces of Isfahan, Yazd, and Markazi in the form of polluting and water-intensive industries must be stopped."

Many independent experts point out that Iran's water crisis will not be solved by transferring new resources. If consumption management is not reformed, if water-intensive agriculture does not change its practices, and if water-intensive industries are not relocated from arid regions, even the largest water transfer projects will only buy time and deepen the current crisis.

🔴ExxonMobil has spent millions of dollars on the local community, yet the people living next to its carbon project are protesting
Exxon's strange social responsibility: millions spent, one unhappy community
✍️Naft Khabar:
🚨ExxonMobil has spent money on the local community, provided equipment to emergency responders, established scholarships, and its employees have put in thousands of hours of volunteer work. On paper, nearly every element of a corporate social responsibility program is there. And yet, some of the people who are supposed to live alongside one of the company's largest carbon storage projects in Texas are protesting, saying their concerns about water, safety, and the future of their community have not been heard enough.
🚨What makes the story of ExxonMobil's Rose project so intriguing is precisely this contradiction: a company that spends money on its host community, while that same community has questions and objections about its project.
🚨Over the course of 13 years, roughly 53 million tons of carbon dioxide are set to be injected deep underground in southeastern Texas. Exxon says the Rose CCS project is part of the solution for cutting emissions from America's heavy industries. But local residents have a simpler question: if the carbon from big industries is going to be buried beneath our land, who can guarantee our water, our safety, and the future of this region?
🚨The Texas Railroad Commission, the state body that regulates oil, gas, and underground storage, issued the project permit in September by a two-to-one vote. The key detail was that the dissenting vote came not from an environmental group, but from one of the commission's own three members.

✅️ Part two and final part of Dr. Mehdi Qamshi's note: Therefore, with this approach, while maintaining readiness to prevent the destructive effects of floods, the country's planning should be steered in a direction where this possible water event is viewed more as an opportunity, and optimal use is made of the water yield resulting from this phenomenon (it should also be noted that in 1398, the output of credible climate prediction models differed, and this very issue caused, or served as the excuse for, surprise — but now that is not the case). In sum, in recent years we have not treated our water resources properly and have created many problems in our country's environmental and territorial foundations, the most important of which can be summarized as: the drying up of the country's important lakes and wetlands such as Hor al-Azim, Shadegan, Gavkhouni, Jazmurian, Hamoun, and Lake Urmia; the severe drop in groundwater levels across the country's important plains and land subsidence; the growth of dust centers; the problem of aquatic and terrestrial life and pollution in the downstream stretches of rivers; and seawater intrusion into rivers. Therefore, now that there is a possibility of a large volume of water falling from the sky, we can welcome it with two approaches. One approach, rooted in fear and threat, is to focus all our efforts on safely channeling the huge volume of water to the sea, which may also alleviate a few of the above-mentioned problems along its path. But the other approach focuses on making the utmost beneficial use of this yield so that we can solve many of the above-mentioned problems beforehand. Pursuing the second approach, which is certainly in the interest of our country's present and future, requires precise planning, structural works, and, more broadly, a change in how we view this phenomenon. Planning for flood spreading, maximum recharge of aquifers in the country's critical plains, the planned channeling of floods toward wetlands, channeling floods toward dust centers, and finally the safe channeling of floods toward downstream areas and the sea — all of this can be seen as the result of shifting our view of El Niño from a curse to a blessing, and can turn our fear of facing it into an opportunity. And in the end, we can ask ourselves: if the predictions come true, will we be good hosts to welcome El Niño's water yield?

Unveiling of the book "Iranian Sustainability: Environment as Life"
A look at the link between sustainable development, the responsible citizen, and public education
Beh-Mehr has for years pursued the approach of "human development, from children's education to good citizens," and regards education as one of the main grounds for shaping responsible behavior toward society and the environment. In this vein, and coinciding with the start of the new school year, the book "Iranian Sustainability: Environment as Life" will be unveiled in the presence of Mohammad Darvish, researcher and environmental activist — a session dedicated to examining the relationship between education, the environment, and sustainable development.
In this session, two central questions will be discussed:
1. If environmental education is part of the path toward educating a responsible citizen, what revisions do educational policymaking and the role of the school, teacher, and assessment methods require?
2. If the environmental crisis is tied to our way of living and decision-making, how can the school help shape a generation with more responsible choices and lifestyles?
We invite those interested to join us in this scientific session.
